synopsis: The corpus treats traceability as essential to usable safety evidence: each run must connect hazard, safety and performance requirements, scenario, test case, result and safety-case evidence, with the exact software and models identifiable [f7105, f12202]. Run manifests should retain immutable identifiers, configuration and calibration versions, seeds, assets, metrics, verdicts and data checksums; configuration control extends to physical machine variants and the current site, not just software [f7108, f7109, f1141, f3831, f11072]. Credible models alone are insufficient: the toolchain must be qualified, controlled and reproducible, and changes must trigger impact analysis or revalidation rather than silently inherit obsolete evidence [f8227, f8048, f8229, f10232]. The G1 gate at the end of January 2027 requires one reproducible end-to-end scenario under configuration control and an unresolved-assumption report, while the plan must define sustainment and revalidation responsibilities after September 2027 [f10197, f10179]. Implementation remains a planning risk: ASAM TestSpecification was still developing infrastructure in October 2026, tool qualification and configuration management can become late blockers, and version drift is rated High risk despite no off-road case being found [f7119, f10351, f11066, f11067].

relations.note: Identical requirements for models replacing physical evidence, despite different attribution labels.
Both require immutable run identifiers for all result-changing ingredients.
Both specify January 2027 G1 and reproducible configuration-controlled execution; chapter adds gate conditions.
Both prescribe freezing procedural-generation ingredients for reproducibility.
Both warn that unfrozen procedural-generation ingredients prevent replay months later.
Run manifest fields operationalize the hazard-to-evidence traceability chain.
Missing provenance prevents identifying the exact product state behind evidence.
Recording guidance adds data-loss counters to exact software and hardware provenance.
Physical machine configuration details identify changes that may invalidate evidence.
Intended versus current physical site differences justify safety-relevant site change control.
Unseen firmware and processing changes justify freezing versions or conducting impact analysis.
High risk assessment lacks a found off-road case; evidential tension, not direct disproof.
Manifest, release and archival controls address the identified irreproducibility risk.
Credibility review tests required control, qualification and independent reproducibility from retained artifacts.
Software-update requalification risk justifies explicit sustainment and revalidation policy.
CARLA-specific frozen qualified build applies the general release-level toolchain freeze.
Required test-management engineering capabilities explain why a simulation engine is not turnkey management.
Omitted toolchain qualification and configuration questions expose potential late programme blockers.
